summary: Describes the security mechanisms for IPv4 and IPv6 and the services they provide. It is the original overall architecture for IPsec as a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2401.

eli5.summary: The master plan for locking and sealing Internet packets, so strangers can't read or change them on the way.

questions: what is the ip security architecture
how does ip authentication header work
what is the difference between ah and esp
subtitle: Encrypting and authenticating IP packets at the network layer

tldr.problem: IP layer has no built-in way to encrypt traffic or authenticate the sender, leaving data vulnerable to eavesdropping and spoofing.
tldr.mechanism: Introduces two headers: Authentication Header (AH) for integrity and authentication, and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) for confidentiality and optionally authentication. Both use cryptographic keys managed by a separate key management protocol.
tldr.outcome: Provides network-layer encryption and authentication transparent to applications. Replaced by RFC 2401 in 1998.

today: RFC 2401 replaced this with a revised security architecture in 1998.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes security mechanisms for IP version 4 (IPv4) and IP version 6 (IPv6). It provides a framework for protecting IP datagrams but does not specify the detailed mechanism for each security algorithm; those are published separately.

The document focuses on IP-layer security rather than application-layer or link-layer security. It defines key management requirements for systems implementing IP security but not the key management protocol itself, leaving that to other standards work.

Three security properties are fundamental: authentication (knowing the data received matches what was sent and confirming the sender), integrity (ensuring data arrives unchanged), and confidentiality (ensuring only intended recipients read the data). Non-repudiation (proving a sender sent something they later deny) may be provided by some authentication algorithms.
sections.eli5: This is the overall plan for protecting IP packets. It does not say exactly how to do it, just where to put the protections and what they should do.

sections.title: Security Headers
sections.content:
Two cryptographic headers protect IP datagrams. The IP Authentication Header (AH) computes a cryptographic authentication function over the datagram using a secret key. It provides integrity and authentication without confidentiality, so it can be widely deployed even in locations where encryption is regulated. Certain fields that change in transit, such as the TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6) field, are omitted from the authentication calculation. AH uses keyed MD5 as the default authentication algorithm with a 128-bit key.

The IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication by encapsulating either an entire IP datagram (tunnel mode) or only the upper-layer data (transport mode) inside an encrypted envelope. Fragmentation and other IP processing occurs after AH processing but before ESP processing. ESP uses DES in CBC mode as the mandatory encryption algorithm for interoperability.

The two headers can be used separately or combined. Using both together provides strong integrity, confidentiality, and authentication. A Security Association is the set of security parameters relating to a connection: the encryption algorithm, the authentication algorithm, the cryptographic keys, and the key lifetime. The combination of a Security Parameter Index (SPI) and destination address uniquely identifies a Security Association.
sections.eli5: Two special headers can be added to packets: AH signs the packet so you know who sent it and nobody changed it. ESP encrypts the packet so nobody can read it. You can use both at once.

sections.title: Key Management
sections.content:
Every IP security implementation must support manual key configuration, where an administrator manually enters the same key on both endpoints. This is practical for small, static networks but does not scale.

Implementations should support an automated key management protocol (such as IKMP or Photuris) once one is published as an Internet standard. Two approaches exist: host-oriented keying, where all users on one host share the same key for traffic to another host, and user-oriented keying, where each user or application has its own key. Host-oriented keying is simpler but vulnerable to attacks from untrusted users on the same host. User-oriented keying should be supported on multi-user systems.

For multicast traffic, key management is complex: multiple senders could share a single key (losing per-sender authentication) or use separate keys (requiring key management for each sender). The document notes that multicast key distribution is an active research area.
sections.eli5: You need to share secret keys with the other end. Someone has to put the keys in, either by hand (simple but tedious) or using a special protocol (not yet standardized in 1995).

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
IP security is useful with firewalls to protect traffic between corporate sites across untrusted networks. A firewall can selectively encrypt traffic destined for other company sites while leaving traffic to public networks unencrypted.

For Quality of Service (QoS) protection, the Authentication Header can authenticate packets for classification within routers, allowing QoS policies to trust packet classification. The IPv6 Flow Identifier combined with AH can help routers ensure each packet receives appropriate handling.

Multi-level secure (MLS) networks transmit data at different sensitivity levels (Unclassified, Secret, etc.) on the same network. AH provides strong authentication for sensitivity labels, preventing attackers from changing a label. ESP with appropriate key management can provide confidentiality for each sensitivity level.

IP Multicast can use IP security with receiver-oriented Security Associations, making the mechanisms well-suited for multicast deployment.
sections.eli5: You can use IP security to make a private tunnel across the internet, protect video calls on shared networks, or ensure secure military networks.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Trade-offs
sections.content:
All IPv6-capable hosts must implement the IP Authentication Header with MD5 using a 128-bit key. IPv4 systems claiming to implement AH must also support keyed MD5 with 128-bit keys. All conforming implementations must support DES in CBC mode for ESP.

Certain encryption transforms without strong integrity mechanisms are vulnerable to cut-and-paste attacks and should not be used unless AH is present.

Security depends entirely on the strength of implemented cryptographic algorithms, the key strength, correct implementation, the security of the key management protocol, and correct implementation of IP security on all participating systems. If multiple senders share a Security Association with a destination, the receiver can only know the packet came from one of them, not which one. Receivers must verify that the claimed source address is valid for the Security Association used.

Use of IP security will increase processor load and latency due to encryption and authentication calculations. However, it should not impact routers or systems not participating in the particular security association.
sections.eli5: The security only works if the math is strong, the keys are good, and everything is implemented correctly. Encryption slows things down a little bit.
